Overview
Client: 30 y/o female, advanced lifter, 20 weeks pregnant, OB cleared for moderate strength training. Contraindications to follow: no supine after week 16 (so all future supine must be avoided), no maximal (near‑max) lifts, avoid breath‑holding/Valsalva, avoid contact sports, and stop any exercise that causes pain, dizziness, lightheadedness, uterine contractions, or vaginal bleeding. Emphasize controlled tempo, RPE 5–7/10 (moderate), increased rest as needed, and heart‑rate monitoring only if clinician has given specific limits — otherwise use perceived exertion and ability to carry conversation. Hydration, frequent breaks, and avoiding prolonged standing without movement are also important.

Program goals
- Maintain and build strength safely (relative to pre‑pregnancy baseline).
- Preserve muscular balance and joint stability as the center of mass shifts.
- Protect the pelvic floor and promote safe loading.
- Maintain aerobic conditioning with low‑impact options.
- Progress gradually across 12 weeks while respecting pregnancy physiology.

Structure
- 12 weeks divided into three 4‑week blocks (Phase A: weeks 1–4; Phase B: weeks 5–8; Phase C: weeks 9–12).
- 3 strength sessions per week (nonconsecutive days), plus 1–2 light aerobic / mobility sessions.
- Each strength session ~45–60 minutes including warm‑up and cooldown.
- Use multi‑joint compound lifts with pregnancy‑appropriate modifications; avoid supine after week 16, so after week 16 substitute with inclined/standing/side‑lying alternatives.
- Load guidance: avoid 1RM testing. Work in rep ranges 6–12 with RPE 5–7. If technique falters, reduce load. Focus on time under tension and controlled eccentric.
- Pelvic floor and breathing: include low‑load pelvic floor training and diaphragmatic breathing; avoid forceful breath holding.
- Recovery and nutrition notes included at the end.

Progression and intensity notes
- Weeks 1–4: Maintain strength with slightly reduced loads compared with pre‑pregnancy max; build movement patterns and core/pelvic floor control. Focus on 3 sets mostly.
- Weeks 5–8: Moderate progression via volume and slight load increases (still submaximal). Introduce more unilateral and stability challenges as tolerated.
- Weeks 9–12: Prioritize loading that feels comfortable with changing posture and balance. Emphasize half‑range or modified variants if full ROM awkward. Continue submaximal loads, slightly lower intensities if fatigued. Keep sessions conservative and emphasize recovery.

Session template (for each strength day)
- Warm‑up (8–10 min): general cardio 4–6 min (brisk walking, stationary bike, elliptical), dynamic mobility: cat/camel, thoracic rotations, ankle circles, hip CARs, band pull‑aparts; one warm‑up set at lighter load for first main lift.
- Main strength work: 3–5 exercises per session — big compound movements first (3–4 sets), accessory work after (2–3 sets).
- Pelvic floor + breathing cueing: include 1–2 drills per session (see examples).
- Cooldown (5–8 min): gentle mobility, diaphragmatic breathing, stretching (avoid prolonged supine; perform side‑lying or seated stretches).

Weekly schedule example
- Monday: Strength A (lower emphasis)
- Tuesday: Light cardio + mobility or rest (20–30 min walk, bike, or pool)
- Wednesday: Strength B (upper emphasis)
- Thursday: Rest or prenatal yoga / mobility
- Friday: Strength C (full‑body / posterior chain emphasis)
- Saturday: Optional light aerobic (30–40 min walk/pool) or rest
- Sunday: Rest

Exercise selection guidelines and substitutions
- No barbell back squats if breath holding/near max; can use goblet, front rack, safety bar, or box squats. Avoid supine barbell bench after week 16 — use incline/standing chest press, machine seated press, or push‑ups on an elevated surface.
- Deadlifts: Romanian and trap bar deadlifts are fine; trap bar allows more upright torso. Reduce range if uncomfortable.
- Rows and pull variations: seated cable rows, single‑arm DB rows, band rows.
- Single‑leg work is valuable for balance: split squats, Bulgarian split squats, stepups.
- Core: avoid heavy loaded Valsalva, deep twisting, or intense abdominal crunching. Use anti‑extension/anti‑rotation drills (pallof press), quadruped and side‑lying work, heel slides to tolerance, modified dead bugs (one limb at a time), and standing core work. Supine abdominal work avoided after week 16.
- Pelvic floor: gentle quick and hold contractions (as advised by pelvic floor phys) and breathing integration. If history of pelvic floor dysfunction, refer to pelvic floor physiotherapist for individualized plan.

Detailed 12‑week plan

Phase A: Weeks 1–4 — stabilization and maintenance (RPE 5–6)
Goals: reestablish technique, pelvic floor engagement, moderate loading, remove supine.

Week 1
Strength A (Lower emphasis)
- Warm‑up 8–10 min
- Trap bar deadlift — 3 sets x 6–8 reps (moderate load, controlled tempo)
- Bulgarian split squat (DB) — 3 x 8 each leg
- Glute bridge (side‑lying march alternative if supine uncomfortable) — 3 x 10–12 (if supine comfortable and < week16; after week16 do single‑leg bridge on floor in side‑lying or standing hip extension)
- Standing calf raise (single or double) — 3 x 12–15
- Pallof press (band) — 3 x 8–10 each side
- Pelvic floor quick + 5‑second hold drills integrated between sets: 2 sets of 8 quicks and 4 holds

Strength B (Upper emphasis)
- Warm‑up 8–10 min
- Seated DB incline press or standing landmine press — 3 x 6–8
- Single‑arm DB row (knee on bench or split stance) — 3 x 8 each
- Band pull‑apart / face pull — 3 x 12–15
- Seated lateral raise — 2 x 12
- Farmer carry (light–moderate) 3 x 30–45 sec (core + grip)
- Modified dead‑bug on incline bench (one limb at a time) — 2 x 8 each side

Strength C (Full body / posterior emphasis)
- Warm‑up
- Front‑rack goblet squat (KB or DB) or box squat — 3 x 6–8
- Romanian deadlift (DB or barbell light) — 3 x 8
- Single‑arm cable row — 3 x 10 each
- Step‑ups (low box) — 2 x 10 each
- Bird‑dog (control and pelvic floor cue) — 3 x 8 each side
- Side‑lying clamshells — 2 x 12 each side

Week 2–4
- Progression: add 1 set on most accessory lifts (where appropriate), or increase reps by 1–2 per set while keeping RPE 5–6. Keep main lifts at 3–4 sets of 6–8. Continue pelvic floor and breathing work every session. Monitor symptoms and adjust.

Phase B: Weeks 5–8 — moderate progression and unilateral emphasis (RPE 6–7)
Goals: slightly increase load/volume, introduce more single‑leg and anti‑rotation stability, keep avoiding supine.

Week 5 (example week; Weeks 5–8 follow this pattern with small progressions)
Strength A (Lower heavy-ish but submax)
- Warm‑up
- Trap bar deadlift or hex bar DL — 4 x 5–6 (moderate; no maximal attempts)
- Bulgarian split squat (DB) — 3 x 8–10
- Glute‑bridge to single‑leg (or standing cable hip extension) — 3 x 10 each
- Seated calf raise — 3 x 12
- Pallof press (tighter band) 3 x 10 each
- Pelvic floor holds 4 x 5 sec and 8 quicks

Strength B (Upper)
- Warm‑up
- Seated machine chest press or incline DB press — 4 x 6–8
- Bent‑over row or chest‑supported row — 3 x 6–8
- Single‑arm landmine press — 3 x 8 each
- Face pulls — 3 x 12–15
- Suitcase carry (DB) — 3 x 30 sec each side
- Standing anti‑extension plank on incline (hands on bench) — 3 x 20–30 sec

Strength C (Posterior chain / full)
- Warm‑up
- Romanian deadlift or single‑leg RDL — 3 x 6–8 (can alternate weeks between bilateral and unilateral)
- Step‑ups (higher but safe) — 3 x 8–10 each
- Pull‑down or assisted pull‑up — 3 x 8–10
- Reverse lunge to balance — 3 x 8 each
- Side plank on knee or incline side‑plank — 3 x 20–30 sec
- Modified bird‑dog progression 3 x 8

Weeks 6–8
- Progression: increase sets to 4 for main lifts on week 7 if tolerated, or increase weight by ~2.5–5% only if RPE stays ≤7. Continue pelvic floor integration. Maintain comfortable aerobic work 20–30 min 1–2x per week.

Phase C: Weeks 9–12 — maintenance with emphasis on comfort, balance, and recovery (RPE 5–7)
Goals: Keep strength and functional capacity through advancing pregnancy, reduce load if necessary, maintain confidence with movement.

Week 9 (example)
Strength A (Lower)
- Warm‑up
- Safety‑bar or goblet squat to box (higher box if more belly) — 3 x 6–8
- Single‑leg RDL (DB) — 3 x 8 each
- Cable hip thrust/standing hip extension — 3 x 10–12
- Seated calf raise or farmer carry on toes 3 x 12
- Pallof press or standing anti‑rotation — 3 x 8–10
- Pelvic floor gentle holds + breathing (integration)

Strength B (Upper)
- Warm‑up
- Seated row machine — 3 x 8
- Incline DB press or standing chest press (cable) — 3 x 8
- Single arm DB row supported — 3 x 8 each
- Band face pull — 3 x 12
- Overhead carry (light) 2 x 30 sec
- Standing "dead‑bug" against wall or on incline — 2 x 10

Strength C (Full / posterior emphasis)
- Warm‑up
- Trap bar DL or light conventional DL — 3 x 5–6
- Split squat (rear foot elevated low) — 3 x 8 each
- Pull‑down / assisted pull‑up — 3 x 8–10
- Glute band walks or side‑lying clams — 2 x 15
- Side plank variation on knee — 2 x 20–30 sec
- Bird‑dog controlled — 2 x 8

Weeks 10–12
- Keep volumes similar or reduce if fatigue rises. Prioritize technique and breathing. If balance becomes problematic, shift to more seated/bench supported variants. Continue mobility and daily walking. In week 12, transition emphasis further toward maintenance: fewer sets (2–3) on main lifts and more emphasis on mobility and pelvic floor.

Special considerations and exercise substitutions (pregnancy‑specific)
- Supine: Avoid supine position after week 16. Replace supine bridges with standing cable hip extensions, side‑lying bridges, or incline-supported glute bridges. Replace supine core work with side‑lying, quadruped, or seated variations.
- Breathing: Instruct diaphragmatic breathing and exhale on effort; avoid long breath holds. Cue exhale on concentric/straining part.
- Pelvic floor: Encourage gentle daily pelvic floor contractions (pelvic floor physiotherapist prescription ideal). Avoid forceful bearing down. Cue pelvic floor engagement during lifts but without prolonged holds.
- Balance: Use support (sturdy bench/rail) when doing single‑leg work as center of mass shifts.
- RPE monitoring: Target RPE 5–7. If heavy fatigue, reduce to RPE 4–5.
- Symptoms: If any pelvic pain, leaking, strong pressure, contractions, dizziness, or bleeding occur, stop exercise and contact OB.

Nutrition & recovery guidance
- Calories: Generally need modestly increased caloric intake in pregnancy; exact needs vary. For an active, strength‑training pregnant client, add approx. +200–300 kcal/day in second trimester and +300–450 kcal/day in third trimester above pre‑pregnancy requirements, adjusted per individual. Prioritize nutrient‑dense foods.
- Protein: Aim 1.2–1.8 g/kg pre‑pregnancy bodyweight per day (higher end if resistance training and to support fetal growth). Spread protein across meals.
- Hydration: Frequent sipping during sessions; avoid overheating. Cool environment and avoid exercising to exhaustion.
- Micronutrients: Continue prenatal multivitamin with folate, iron as prescribed, adequate calcium and vitamin D. Encourage iron‑rich foods if anemic.
- Rest: 7–9 hours nightly, naps as needed. Increase recovery between sessions if fatigued.
- Pelvic floor & postpartum prep: Gentle pelvic floor exercises during pregnancy help recovery postpartum. Consider referral to pelvic floor phys for individualized dosing.

Monitoring and red flags to stop exercise
- Any vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, unusual or severe abdominal pain, regular painful contractions, dizziness, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, decreased fetal movement (later pregnancy) — stop and seek medical attention per OB.
- Excessive uterine pressure or incontinence worsening — reassess load and referral.

Notes for the trainer
- Keep communication open; daily wellbeing and sleep/fatigue will change loading capacity. Encourage client to self‑regulate.
- Reinforce no heavy Valsalva — coach breathing through sets.
- Use objective modifiers: if poor recovery, reduce to 2 strength sessions and 1 light session weekly, or reduce sets by ~30%.
- Consider brief consultation with client’s OB or pelvic floor physiotherapist for tailored pelvic floor progressions, especially if history of pelvic floor issues.

If you’d like, I can:
- Convert this into a printable week‑by‑week sheet with weights and progression suggestions based on her current 1RM estimates (we’ll use percentages but remain conservative).
- Provide a list of specific warm‑up and pelvic floor cueing scripts you can use while coaching.
- Customize the plan to accommodate any history of diastasis recti, pelvic floor dysfunction, or prior injuries.

Would you like a printable 12‑week calendar with daily sessions and suggested example loads based on estimated pre‑pregnancy 1RMs?
